item.title: China's spies set sights on AI semiconductors years before Nvidia scandal
item.description: China's espionage agency has been running a secret campaign to help the country's companies acquire advanced AI chips and to gather intelligence on the sector, officials say ...
item.dc:creator: NYT
item.content:encoded: By Chris Buckley and Julian E Barnes When China’s top espionage agency updated its priorities this year, it added a revealing goal: overcoming Western barriers to technologies that Xi Jinping sees as crucial to China’s rise. At the heart of that quest are the advanced semiconductors needed to power artificial intelligence, including chips that the United States has barred US companies like Nvidia from exporting to China. China must “adopt extraordinary measures to intensify the drive for core technologies in priority sectors,” Xi told the Politburo, a council of senior officials, in January, according to an official text of his speech. “As swiftly as possible, solve the ‘chokehold’ problems holding back development of future industries.” The spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, has long been dedicated to eliminating threats to Communist Party rule in China. Now, it has made it a priority to acquire advanced semiconductor chips and gather intelligence about them, according to several serving and former security and intelligence officials from governments outside China in Asia, the United States and Europe. How China’s spy agency is seeking to obtain advanced chips and intelligence about them has become a central question in the case of Alice Huang. She is a Chinese businesswoman whom US officials say the Chinese agency was working with to spy on Jensen Huang, the chief executive of the American chip giant Nvidia, allegations that were first reported by The New York Times. Huang has not responded to requests for comment, and China has rejected the claims of espionage as “pure fabrication.” The Chinese spy agency’s campaign to acquire chips, details of which have not been previously reported, has been underway for at least two years, according to the current and former officials. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence. Among the campaign’s main elements: - The head of the spy agency, Chen Yixin, who holds the title of minister of state security, created a working team that is leading the effort and reports directly to him, multiple foreign officials said. Chen has worked under Xi since they were officials in Zhejiang Province in eastern China, a cradle of China’s high-tech boom.- The group was assigned to help China’s “counter-blockade” work — efforts to overcome export controls imposed by the United States and its allies.- The campaign includes helping Chinese companies acquire and smuggle advanced chips into China.- The group also collects intelligence about the semiconductor sector and its supply chains, according to several officials briefed on the campaign.In April, Chen unveiled the new mission. “Deepen the struggle against blockades, and comprehensively advance artificial intelligence innovation, industry development, and applications,” Chen wrote in a Communist Party journal. “Focus on tackling the ‘chokeholds’ of critical technologies,” he wrote, and solve the problem of technologies that “cannot be obtained by asking, buying or pleading.” “Chen is signalling to the party leadership and his own ranks that his agency is elevating AI competition with the US as a long-term, top priority,” said Alex Joske, the managing director of security practice at Garnaut Global, a consultancy firm, who studies the Chinese security apparatus. “He is telling his officers to find more ways to wage this struggle.” A Central Strategy The ministry’s campaign is part of a wider push by the ruling Communist Party to overcome Western-imposed restrictions on critical technology. China is determined to close its gap with the United States in the computing capacity needed for progress in artificial intelligence. At the top, that effort is being coordinated by the Central Science and Technology Commission. The commission is a secretive Communist Party organ that Xi established in 2023. This was not long after the US Commerce Department, in late 2022, started banning exports of Nvidia’s advanced chips directly to China, out of concern that the chips could help Beijing crack American encryption and design new weapons. The party commission is ranked higher than ministries and is led by Ding Xuexiang, one of only seven members of the Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee, its inner circle of power. “Computing power is a major indicator of overall national power,” Ding said in May when he visited energy and computing facilities in Beijing and nearby regions that are part of a planned nationwide AI computing network, according to Xinhua, China’s official news agency. Xi created the commission to better marshal the country’s scientists, institutes, labs across ministries and companies for national priorities such as achieving technological self-reliance. The commission rarely surfaces in Chinese news reports; its budgets and plans are not made public. But it has become an engine of Xi’s plans for technological pre-eminence, said Christopher K Johnson, a former Central Intelligence Agency analyst focused on China. The director of the commission, Ding, has long been a close aide to Xi and is also a vice-premier overseeing science and technology policy. The Spy Agency’s ‘Anti-Blockade Struggle’ China’s espionage service and other parts of the government have for decades pursued technology and research from abroad, using both open and illicit methods. But under Xi, that effort assumed greater urgency, with more top-level coordination, including in artificial intelligence, several experts said. Throughout this year, Chen, the agency’s chief, has repeatedly said the “anti-blockade struggle” is one of the key duties of China’s Ministry of State Security. “Certain countries are going to every length to impose a ‘chokehold’ on China in fields of critical technology,” Chen wrote in a party journal last year. “Technology competition among the major powers has entered its most intense, most strenuous and most critical phase of close-quarters combat.” As American companies, followed by Chinese ones, developed successively powerful AI models, officials in Beijing have increasingly recognised the potential for artificial intelligence to threaten their power at home and abroad, said Gregory C Allen, the founder and chief executive of Decision Tree Research, a firm that specialises in AI and other advanced technologies. In September, Chen himself referred to US tech companies and their AI models — like Claude Mythos and GPT-5.5-Cyber — as examples of new cybersecurity threats, as he described the risks that AI posed to the party’s hold on power. “China’s senior leadership understands that AI is critically, strategically essential, and that leadership in AI is obviously related to leadership in semiconductors,” said Allen, a former senior official at the US Department of Defense’s Joint Artificial Intelligence Center. Chen became the state security minister in late 2022, and just over a year later, the ministry issued a warning that AI was “highly likely in the near future to profoundly transform the national security landscape.” In 2024, the ministry said that its officers were scoring successes against the attempts of “the United States and other Western countries to lock us in at the low-end” of technology. The Role of Businesses and Other Groups China has sometimes used front organisations or researchers to collect information about foreign AI technology, said Joske, the consultant. “M.S.S. is very comfortable using business covers,” he said, “and it’s very comfortable running people as assets without directly telling those people that they’re working for the M.S.S.” Such covers could include organisations ostensibly focused on academic research. In September, MI5, the British security agency, asserted that a Chinese research institute linked to the Chinese spy agency had drawn in British scientists for research that, apparently unbeknown to the scientists, “directly improves M.S.S. technical capability for espionage.” Companies such as the one Alice Huang founded, Megaspeed, are viewed as another potential vehicle for gathering intelligence. The precise nature of Alice Huang’s role in the ministry’s chip effort remains unclear. US officials say Huang, who was having an affair with the Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, passed information to Beijing about him. The US government is also investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling advanced chips into China. Megaspeed, which is based in Singapore, bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips and entered the business of providing high-end computing capacity to Chinese companies. Such services have allowed Chinese businesses to use Nvidia chips at data centres abroad by sidestepping US rules that ban sales of the most advanced AI chips directly to Chinese firms. Last week, The Times also reported that Megaspeed was possibly aiding a lab with links to China’s military, through Alibaba, the Chinese internet giant. Alibaba is a customer and financial backer of Megaspeed. Providing Nvidia chips to support research for China’s military would be a violation of US law. An Alibaba spokeswoman said: “Any suggestions that Alibaba provides services to the military is groundless. Alibaba Cloud’s service agreement strictly prohibits the use of our products and services for any military purpose.” In an effort to address what many in Washington see as a loophole, the Trump administration announced on Monday that it would move ahead with a new rule to prevent China from being able to access advanced semiconductors from Nvidia and other US companies through the use of data centres outside China. The new restriction will require overseas data centres to obtain a government licence before supplying “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in countries on a list that includes China, Russia and Iran. It goes into effect in about 90 days. The restriction could make China’s pursuit of self-reliance more urgent, a goal Xi has cast as a fight for survival, echoing the party’s revolutionary past. “Like the Red Army on the Long March, we’re now on a new Long March,” he told technicians while visiting an AI data hub under construction in northern China last month. He was referring to a gruelling trek taken by Communist troops in the 1930s that cemented Mao’s leadership of the revolution. “You are an army in the drive for advanced technological self-reliance.”

item.title: Oil, gas import bill up 60% in Oct as Brent surges, LPG use declines
item.description: Direct private LPG imports fell 83.8 per cent in October and 97.3 per cent in April-October. Packed domestic LPG sales by state-run companies fell 11.8 per cent in October, and bulk LPG sales fell ...
item.dc:creator: Press Trust of India
item.content:encoded: India's net oil and gas import bill rose 60 per cent year-on-year to $16 billion in October as Brent crude averaged $124.77 a barrel, almost double that of a year earlier, according to data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), part of the oil ministry.The net bill was $10.0 billion in October 2025. Crude imports alone cost $19.5 billion, against $10.4 billion a year ago, even though volumes rose only 11 per cent to 23.3 million tonnes. LNG imports cost $1.3 billion, and petroleum product exports brought in $6.3 billion.Brent averaged $116.77 in September and $64.75 in October 2025. The Indian basket averaged $119.91 in October, against $65.08 a year earlier.Over April-October, the net import bill reached $97.7 billion, up from $70.3 billion a year earlier. Crude imports rose 2.7 per cent in volume but cost $111.0 billion, against $72.3 billion.Consumption of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) fell 12.3 per cent in October and 15.1 per cent in April-October. The number of active domestic LPG customers stood at 32.6 crore on November 1, down from 33.4 crore on April 1, the PPAC data showed.Direct private LPG imports fell 83.8 per cent in October and 97.3 per cent in April-October. Packed domestic LPG sales by state-run companies fell 11.8 per cent in October, and bulk LPG sales fell 49.1 per cent. Auto LPG sales rose 23.9 per cent.Imports of petroleum products fell 41.2 per cent in October and 49.3 per cent in the fiscal year so far. PPAC attributed the fiscal-year decline mainly to lower imports of LPG, pet coke and fuel oil.The International Energy Agency said in its World Energy Outlook 2026 that LPG imports fell by over 50 per cent in the first two months of shipping disruption through the Strait of Hormuz.Other fuels held up better. Diesel consumption rose 12 per cent in October to 8.5 million tonnes, petrol rose 3.5 per cent, and bitumen rose 16.5 per cent. Total petroleum product consumption rose 2.7 per cent to 20.5 million tonnes in October. It was still down 3.2 per cent in April-October at 134.2 million tonnes.Natural gas consumption fell 7.27 per cent to 5,707 million standard cubic metres in October. LNG imports fell 6.94 per cent to 3,014 million standard cubic metres.India processed 24.1 million tonnes of crude in October, up 7.1 per cent, or about 5.70 million barrels a day. Of that, 22.0 million tonnes were imported crude, and domestic output was 2.1 million tonnes. Imports met 88.7 per cent of crude consumption in October.Domestic crude and condensate output was 2.3 million tonnes. Import dependency for natural gas stood at 52.8 per cent in October.Ethanol blending in petrol stood at 20 per cent in October, PPAC data showed.

item.description: UN climate negotiations at COP31 in Turkey face a breakdown after the summit president ruled out a fresh draft agreement amid a lack of consensus among countries.

COP31 climate talks set to collapse without a political agreement UN climate negotiations at COP31 in Turkey face a breakdown after the summit president ruled out a fresh draft agreement amid a lack of consensus among countries.

COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, face uncertainty as countries remain divided over the proposed agreement, with the summit president ruling out a fresh draft text. | Image: Reuters

Reuters 1 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 7:01 PM IST

Listen to This Article

UN climate talks in Turkey looked ??set to collapse without a political agreement after COP31 summit president Murat Kurum said there would be no new draft of the deal.   Earlier, multiple countries and negotiating blocs said they could not accept the version of the text put before them.   "There will be no new text ??from now on. We will not be carrying out work on a new text in an environment where there is no consensus," Kurum said.   More From This Section

item.description: Google has pledged $5 million to IIT Kharagpur to strengthen advanced artificial intelligence (AI) research, expand educational opportunities and develop the next generation of technology ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / News / Google pledges $5 million to IIT Kharagpur for advanced AI research

Google pledges $5 million to IIT Kharagpur for advanced AI research The announcement was made during the institute's platinum jubilee celebrations on November 21

The funding will primarily support applied AI research in areas such as Indic languages, agriculture, materials science and educational technology (Photo: Reuters)

Press Trust of India Kolkata 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 1:39 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Google has pledged $5 million to IIT Kharagpur to strengthen advanced artificial intelligence (AI) research, expand educational opportunities and develop the next generation of technology professionals, a senior institute official said on Sunday. The announcement was made during the institute's platinum jubilee celebrations on November 21. IIT Kharagpur Director Suman Chakraborty told PTI that Sundar Pichai, an alumnus and CEO of Google, played a key role in facilitating the funding for IIT Kharagpur. " We are proud of him (Sundar Pichai) as an alumnus who heads Google. We are thankful to Google for pledging the money, and Pichai assisted in IIT Kharagpur getting the money," he said.   The funding will primarily support applied AI research in areas such as Indic languages, agriculture, materials science and educational technology. Also Read

Google announces $5 mn funding for IIT Kharagpur for advanced AI research

The grant will be channelled through three broad areas -- advanced AI research, educational opportunities, including expansion of AI training and curriculum for students and faculty, and capacity building through the development of campus AI infrastructure, frameworks and tools. The director said another alumnus, Jyoti Chatterjee, had pledged an additional $5 million as seed endowment for developing a next-generation data initiative. "The contributions are expected to provide a major boost to the institute's efforts to expand AI-driven innovation and enhance its role in developing skilled technology professionals," he said.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
